findings.name: Missing Secure Attribute on Sensitive Session Cookie
findings.description: The session cookie 'tops_technologies_session' is set without the 'Secure' attribute. This cookie governs user state and authentication sessions. Without the 'Secure' attribute, the browser may transmit this sensitive cookie over unencrypted HTTP connections if mixed-content links are loaded or if the user types the HTTP version of the URL, exposing the session identifier to interception via network-level eavesdropping or Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks.
findings.impact: Session hijacking and unauthorized account access to user or administrative profiles.
findings.remediation: Configure the application framework or web server to enforce the 'Secure' attribute on all session and sensitive cookies. In PHP/Laravel configurations, set 'secure' to true in config/session.php or adjust php.ini settings: 'session.cookie_secure = On'.

findings.name: Deprecated Clickjacking Protection Directives (X-Frame-Options ALLOW-FROM)
findings.description: The application sends the 'X-Frame-Options' header configured with the 'ALLOW-FROM' directive. Modern browsers have deprecated and no longer support 'ALLOW-FROM', causing them to either ignore the header entirely or fallback to insecure configurations. While Content-Security-Policy (CSP) 'frame-ancestors' is also present, legacy clients and scrapers that do not interpret CSP correctly remain vulnerable to UI redressing (Clickjacking).
findings.impact: Attackers can frame the target website on legacy browsers, potentially tricking users into performing unintended administrative or account actions.
findings.remediation: Remove the obsolete 'X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM' header. Rely entirely on the 'Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors' directive for clickjacking protection. In Nginx, replace the header with: add_header Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'self' www.learnvern.com;" always;

findings.name: Administrative Portal Exposure and Route Sprawl
findings.description: Multiple distinct administrative paths (/wp-admin/, /admin/, and /panel/) are exposed publicly and return successful response codes (200 OK). Web Application Firewalls or directory brute-force protections are not currently restricting access to these paths. This sprawl increases the threat surface, permitting automated credential-stuffing campaigns and vulnerability scanning against sensitive management consoles.
findings.impact: Facilitates brute-force attacks and vulnerability exploitation against administrative interfaces, potentially resulting in full system compromise.
findings.remediation: Implement strict IP-based access controls on administrative paths in the Nginx configuration. For example: location ~ ^/(wp-admin|admin|panel) { allow 192.168.1.0/24; deny all; }
